name: Voice Timbre Analysis
description: Analyzes vocal timbre characteristics including harmonic richness and formant transitions for voice synthesis detection.
algorithm: Spectral Envelope and Harmonic Timbre Forensics
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or cloned voices by analyzing the spectral envelope and harmonic structure of the voice — the timbral fingerprint that makes each voice unique:

1. **Harmonic Structure Analysis**: The method extracts fundamental frequency (F0) and harmonics up to the 40th partial using a harmonic product spectrum (HPS) approach. For each voiced frame, a harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR) profile is computed per frequency band: HNR = 10 log₁₀(Eharmonic / Enoise) dB. Natural voices show characteristic HNR decay with increasing harmonic number — typically 25–35 dB at H1, decreasing to 5–15 dB by H20. The spectral tilt (roll-off rate) follows approximately −12 dB/octave for modal voice but varies predictably with phonation type: breathy (−18 dB/octave), pressed (−6 dB/octave). AI-generated voices often show: (a) too-uniform HNR decay across harmonics, (b) spectral tilt that doesn't vary naturally with loudness changes (the Lombard effect should steepen tilt by 2–4 dB/octave), or (c) harmonic amplitudes that follow a smooth mathematical function rather than the irregular peaks caused by vocal tract resonances.

2. **Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC) Dynamics**: Beyond static MFCC features, the method analyzes MFCC trajectories over time. 13 MFCCs plus their delta and delta-delta coefficients are computed with 25-ms frames and 10-ms hop. The modulation spectrum of each MFCC coefficient is then calculated — the spectral content of how each cepstral coefficient varies over time. Natural speech shows a dominant modulation peak at 3–5 Hz (corresponding to syllabic rate) with secondary peaks at 1–2 Hz (prosodic phrases). The modulation transfer function (MTF) should show a low-pass characteristic with a cutoff around 16 Hz, reflecting articulatory constraints. AI-generated speech may show: missing or shifted modulation peaks, overly smooth modulation spectra (lacking the stochastic variability of natural articulatory movements), or modulation energy at frequencies above the articulatory cutoff.

3. **Jitter, Shimmer, and Microprosodic Analysis**: Natural voices exhibit cycle-to-cycle perturbations in pitch (jitter) and amplitude (shimmer) due to the biomechanical properties of vocal fold vibration. The method computes: local jitter (average absolute period difference / mean period, normal range: 0.1–1.0%), shimmer (average absolute amplitude difference / mean amplitude, normal range: 0.4–3.5%), and harmonic-to-noise ratio (normal: > 20 dB for sustained vowels). Additionally, microprosodic effects are analyzed: consonantal perturbation of F0 (voiced consonants lower F0 by 5–15 Hz relative to adjacent vowels), intrinsic vowel pitch (high vowels /i,u/ have F0 2–10 Hz higher than low vowel /a/), and syllable-final lengthening. AI voices frequently show: jitter/shimmer values that are too low (overly clean) or too consistent (not varying naturally with loudness and pitch), and absence of microprosodic effects that arise from physical coupling between articulation and phonation.

4. **Long-Term Average Spectrum (LTAS) and Speaker Formant**: The LTAS is computed over the entire speech sample using 1/3-octave smoothing. This reveals the speaker formant — a cluster of energy in the 2.5–3.5 kHz region (for trained speakers) or 3–4 kHz (for untrained speakers) caused by the piriform fossa and laryngeal vestibule. The method checks: (a) LTAS should show a spectral peak at the speaker formant frequency that remains stable across different phonetic contexts, (b) the overall LTAS slope should be approximately −6 to −9 dB/octave above 500 Hz, (c) the 2–5 kHz region should show the characteristic individual spectral profile that varies between speakers but remains consistent within a speaker. AI-generated voices may produce LTAS profiles that lack a clear speaker formant, show an inconsistent spectral shape across different utterances, or present a generic LTAS that doesn't match any specific vocal tract configuration.
parameters:
Harmonic analysis: up to 40th partial
HNR profile: per-band, 25-ms frames
Spectral tilt: −12 dB/octave (modal voice)
MFCC: 13 coefficients + Δ + ΔΔ, 25-ms frame, 10-ms hop
Modulation spectrum: 0–20 Hz range
Jitter threshold: 0.1–1.0% (normal)
Shimmer threshold: 0.4–3.5% (normal)
HNR threshold: > 20 dB (sustained vowels)
LTAS smoothing: 1/3-octave bands
Minimum analysis duration: 10 seconds of voiced speech
accuracy: 83–91% accuracy detecting AI-generated speech via timbre analysis. MFCC modulation spectrum achieves AUC of 0.90. Jitter/shimmer analysis provides F1-score of 0.85 for neural TTS detection. LTAS speaker formant consistency adds 2–4% improvement. Performance varies with speech duration and recording quality.
source: Tirumala, S. S. et al. (2017). Speaker Identification Features Extraction Methods. IEEE ICCSP.
useCase: Detecting AI voice cloning and neural TTS through spectral timbre inconsistencies. Forensic speaker verification using harmonic structure uniqueness. Identifying synthetic voices in deepfake videos. Quality assessment of voice conversion output.
strengths:
• Captures the unique spectral fingerprint of individual voices
• Jitter/shimmer analysis exploits fundamental biomechanical voice properties
• MFCC modulation spectrum is robust across recording conditions
• LTAS provides a holistic view of voice characteristics over long durations
• Multiple independent timbre features provide complementary detection
limitations:
• Requires at least 10 seconds of continuous voiced speech for reliable LTAS
• Recording quality and microphone characteristics affect harmonic analysis
• Emotional speech and singing have different jitter/shimmer ranges than modal voice
• Codec compression (MP3, AAC) alters high-frequency harmonic amplitudes
• State-of-the-art neural TTS models are producing increasingly natural timbre
